\nMETHODS
Study population
The study population consisted of partici-
pants of the 1990 Nova Scotia Nutrition
Survey. A sample of 3,684 non-institution-
alized individuals between the ages of 
18-74 and stratified by age, sex, and coun-
ty were identified among registrants of the
Nova Scotia Medical Services Insurance.21
Among the 2,777 (75%) individuals who
were located, 2,198 (79%) individuals
agreed to participate and completed the
survey.21 Nine individuals were excluded
from the present study since they had a
myocardial infarction incident in the year
prior to the interview.
Dietary and risk factor assessment
The Nova Scotia Nutrition Survey was
conducted in 1990 and consisted of a face-
to-face interview, including a 24-hour
dietary recall questionnaire, a modified
food frequency questionnaire, and ques-
tions on demographics, socioeconomic sta-
tus, and other risk factors including smok-
ing and diabetes.21 Macro and micro-
nutrients in these individuals’ diets were
calculated using the Canadian Dietary
Information 
software 
program.21
Hemeiron was estimated as 40% of the
iron in meat, fish, and poultry.20,22-24 Body
Mass Index (BMI) was calculated by divid-
ing weight in kilograms by the square of
height in meters.
Health outcomes
All Nova Scotia administrative health
records from 1989 onwards are stored at
the Population Health Research Unit of
Dalhousie University.25 Incidence of non-
fatal and fatal acute myocardial infarction
(ICD-9 code 410) was obtained by linking
participants with these administrative data-
bases, including hospital discharge records,
physician visits, and vital statistics.
Information up to the end of the 1998 cal-
endar year was included in the analyses.
The linkage procedure also revealed out-
of-province migration of 206 participants,
and their information was included until
the date of migration.
Data analysis
We adjusted for the intake of iron and
hemeiron for the total energy intake
(iron/hemeiron intake per 1000 Kcal).26,27
This adjustment was suggested by Willet et
al. on the basis of a higher correlation
between subsequent nutrition surveys
when adjusted for caloric intake.28 We
divided study participants into tertiles
based on energy-adjusted intake of iron
and hemeiron. The lowest intake group
was used as the reference group. Age was
considered as a continuous covariate and
divided by 10 to quantify the impact of
10-year age increments. Similarly, energy
intake was considered as a continuous
covariate and the impact of 1000 Kcal
increments was examined. We applied
logistic regressions with myocardial infarc-
tion (nonfatal and fatal combined) as the
dependent variable. In initial analyses, we
adjusted for age and gender. In subsequent
analyses, we further adjusted for estab-
lished confounders including smoking,
BMI, diabetes, income, total fat, saturated
fat, and cholesterol. Sample weights are
generally applied in the analysis of surveys
with stratified sampling. For longitudinal
analysis of survey data with follow-up,
Korn and Graubard recommend adjusting
for the variables used in defining the sam-
ple weights (age, gender, and county) and
not incorporating sample weights.29 We
applied these recommendations in all
analyses. However, since county did not
substantially affect any of our estimates of
interest, we excluded this covariate from
our analyses.30
RESULTS
During the eight years following the sur-
vey, 94 (4.3%) individuals had an acute
myocardial infarction incident, of which
17 were fatal. Table I presents demograph-
ic and dietary characteristics of participants
with and without myocardial infarctions.
The study participants had a mean iron
intake of 6.95 mg per 1000 Kcal and a
mean hemeiron intake of 0.65 mg per
1000 Kcal (Table I). Adjusting for age and
gender differences, individuals in the high-
est iron intake tertile had 0.67 times the
risk of an acute myocardial infarction com-
pared to those in the lowest iron intake ter-
tile (95% CI of 0.40 to 1.15). Individuals

\nin the highest hemeiron intake tertile had
0.69 times the risk of an acute myocardial
infarction compared to those in the lowest
hemeiron intake tertile (95% CI of 0.41 to
1.17). In other words, the risk for myocar-
dial infarction is less among individuals
with high iron or high hemeiron intake,
although these differences are not statisti-
cally significant. Statistically significant dif-
ferences were obtained with respect to age
and gender: each 10-year increment in age
more than doubled the risk of myocardial
infarction, while females had 0.63 times
the risk of males. In addition, individuals
with diabetes and limited education had a
higher risk of myocardial infarction.
Smokers and individuals with low income
and high BMI also had a greater risk of
myocardial infarction, but the associations
were not statistically significant (Table I).
Table II presents the risk for myocardial
infarction associated with iron/hemeiron
intake when simultaneously adjusted for
the following confounders: age, gender,
smoking, BMI, diabetes, income, dietary
lipids, saturated fat, and cholesterol. The
risk of myocardial infarction for individu-
als in higher iron and hemeiron intake ter-
tiles was less than that of individuals in the
lowest intake tertiles, but these associations
were not statistically significant.
All the above results were almost identi-
cal when the analyses were further adjusted
for the length of follow-up as a means to
control for the 206 participants who
moved out of province (results not shown).
DISCUSSION
We found no increased risk for myocardial
infarction among individuals with high
iron or high hemeiron intake. Rather, indi-
viduals with higher iron and hemeiron
intake seemed to be at lower risk for
myocardial infarction, but these associa-
tions were not statistically significant.
Diet is cultural, and there are major dif-
ferences between countries and regions.
Therefore, it is important to investigate
dietary patterns and risks locally. Intake of
iron and hemeiron in the Nova Scotia
population appeared to be lower than in
the European study20 that reported an
increased risk of myocardial infarction
with increased hemeiron intake. The high-
er risk in the European study may be
attributable to high hemeiron intake and
high risk of nonfatal myocardial infarctions
in their highest tertile, since there were no
substantial risk differences between their
lowest and medium tertiles. With lower
hemeiron intake among the Nova Scotia
population, our study participants would
primarily fall in the lower and middle ter-
tiles of the European sample, with only
very few in their highest tertile. We specu-
late that this may be the reason that the
two studies have different results. With
respect to the risk associated with iron, our
results are consistent with those of a previ-
ous Canadian study among participants of
a nutrition survey conducted between
1970 and 1972,16 and with two other
North American studies among older pop-
ulations.8,9
The Nova Scotia Nutrition Survey was
conducted during spring and fall in order
to account for seasonal variations in diet.
The survey was also designed to obtain
representative samples from different age
groups, sex, and geographical regions of
the province.21 The study is further
strengthened by the high response rate and
the high follow-up rate that was estab-
lished through linkages with administrative
health information. In addition to demon-
strating the absence of a risk for myocar-
dial infarction associated with high dietary
iron and hemeiron intake, the study con-
firms the higher risk of myocardial infarc-
tion for those with diabetes, limited
income and education, smoking and high
BMI for this study population. A limita-
tion in this respect is our inability to adjust
for other risk factors including physical
activity, chronic diseases other than dia-
betes, family history of cardiovascular dis-
ease, and occurrence of a cardiovascular
disease incident prior to 1989.
Individuals with a high caloric intake are
more likely to have a larger amount of iron
and other nutrients in their diet.
According to Willett et al., individuals may
under- or overestimate their food con-
sumption, and thus, nutrient intakes may
be more appropriately estimated as a pro-
portion rather than an absolute amount.28
As pointed out by Hampl et al., consump-
tion of nutrients is partially dependent on
total energy intake, and the density of the
nutrient in the diet is more relevant than
the actual gross intake.26 An energy-adjusted
analysis may also be more appropriate in
terms of public health policy, as it is easier
for an individual to change food items
rather than to change their appetite.
Nevertheless, analyses of absolute iron or
hemeiron intake (not shown) revealed risk
estimates for myocardial infarction similar
to those presented here.
In Canada and most industrialized coun-
tries, cardiovascular disease is the leading
cause of death for both men and women.
In 1997, cardiovascular disease accounted
for 37% of all deaths, with 38% of the
deaths in women and 36% of the deaths in
men.31 In Canada in 1993, the direct costs
of CVD were estimated to be $7.27 billion
while the indirect costs were estimated at
$12.37 billion.32 In Nova Scotia in 1997,
1,589 individuals died from ischemic heart
disease, 806 of these from acute myocardial
infarction.31 The health of Nova Scotians is
among the poorest of all provinces and par-
allels poor lifestyle and socioeconomic fac-
tors.33-35 Clearly, the potential health and
monetary benefits associated with national
and provincial public health interventions
are tremendous.

\nThis study is the first study in Canada to
investigate the importance of both dietary
iron and hemeiron for the risk of myocar-
dial infarction. We found no increased risk
associated with dietary iron and hemeiron
intake, and thus there is no need for imme-
diate action towards changing the current
public health message promoting the con-
sumption of lean meat, which is rich in
iron and hemeiron. The current public
health message should be reconsidered if
the net benefits gained from reducing the
dietary iron and hemeiron intake outweigh
the risks associated with iron deficiency
and with greater intake of meat high in fat
and cholesterol. Since our findings are
based on the lifestyle and diet of Nova
Scotians, which is potentially different
from that of other provincial residents,
there is a need to repeat and confirm our
findings in other parts of the country.

DIETARY IRON AS A RISK FACTOR FOR MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION
RÉSUMÉ
Contexte : Des études épidémiologiques et expérimentales ont suggéré que de hauts niveaux de fer
diététique peuvent mener à un accident du myocarde. La viande maigre, une source importante de
fer diététique, est favorisée, grâce à un niveau de graisse et de cholestérol relativement bas. Cela
nous met-il en danger d’avoir un infarctus du myocarde et devrions-nous reconsidérer la promotion
de la viande maigre?
Méthode : Nous avons examiné la relation entre le fer diététique ou érythrocytaire et le risque d’un
infarctus aigu du myocarde parmi 2 198 participants d’une enquête alimentaire à la Nouvelle-
Écosse.
Résultats : Parmi ces individus, il y a eu 94 incidents d’infarctus aigus du myocarde pendant une
période de huit ans. Ayant ajusté pour les variables confondants, nous n’avons trouvé aucune
augmentation du risque d’un infarctus aigu associée avec une ration alimentaire élevée en fer
diététique et érythrocytaire.
Conclusions : Étant donné le style de vie et les habitudes alimentaires des Néo-Écossais, il n’y a pas
lieu de reconsidérer la promotion de la viande maigre.

Dietary Iron as a Risk Factor for
Myocardial Infarction
Public Health Considerations for Nova Scotia
Darshaka Malaviarachchi, MSc
Paul J. Veugelers, PhD
Alexandra M. Yip, MSc, OT(C)
David R. MacLean, MD
ABSTRACT
Background: Epidemiological and experimental studies have suggested that high levels of
dietary iron and hemeiron can lead to myocardial injury. Lean meat, a primary source of
iron and hemeiron, is promoted because it is lower in fat and cholesterol. Does lean meat
put us at risk for myocardial infarction, and should we reconsider its promotion?
Methods: We analyzed the importance of dietary iron and hemeiron as a risk for
myocardial infarction among 2,198 Nova Scotians who participated in a nutrition survey
and who were followed for eight years, using logistic regression.
Results: Acute myocardial infarction incidents occurred in 94 (4.3%) participants. We
found no increased risk for myocardial infarction associated with high intake of iron and
hemeiron.
Conclusions: Based on Nova Scotian data showing no increased risk for myocardial
infarction with high intake of iron and hemeiron, there is no need for immediate
reconsideration of promotion of lean meat.
A
large portion of the Western diet
consists of meat, and other parts of
the world are moving towards a
Western diet. Within the Western diet,
meat is the primary source of iron.
Recommendations for iron intake are 11 mg
for 14 to 18 year old males and 8 mg for
adult males.1 For females, recommenda-
tions are 15 mg for ages 14 to 18, 18 mg
for ages 19 to 50, and 8 mg for those over
50 years.1 These recommendations can
generally be met with a North American
diet.
Animal experiments have demonstrated
that high amounts of dietary iron can lead
to myocardial injury.2,3 In 1981, Sullivan
proposed that higher incidence of heart dis-
ease in men and postmenopausal women
was due to higher levels of stored iron.4 A
Finnish study in 1992 reinforced that
serum ferritin was associated with risk of
acute myocardial infarction.5 It has since
been shown that a high intake of iron and
cholesterol simultaneously could cause
more severe atherosclerotic lesions than
high intake of cholesterol alone.6 In addi-
tion, high iron levels may have a greater
impact on risk of myocardial infarction in
the presence of diabetes, hypertension, and
smoking.6 The various epidemiological
studies that evaluated serum iron levels and
dietary iron, however, have been inconsis-
tent with respect to the risk for myocardial
infarction.7-20 A recent European study sug-
gested that dietary hemeiron is associated
with increased incidence of myocardial
infarction.20 This finding may have impor-
tant public health implications because cur-
rent health promotion activities advocate
reducing the consumption of meat rich in
fat and cholesterol which implies the pro-
motion of lean meat. Lean meat has a high
iron content, of which approximately 40%
constitutes hemeiron. The promotion of
lean meat may have unforeseen negative
health consequences if hemeiron puts con-
sumers at risk for myocardial infarction.
Therefore, it is important to confirm the
findings of the European study, particularly
in settings that differ with respect to dietary
habits and lifestyle risk factors. In the pre-
sent study, we investigate dietary iron and
hemeiron in relation to the risk of myocar-
dial infarction in the province of Nova
Scotia, using the 1990 Nova Scotia
Nutrition Survey and eight years of follow-
up on myocardial infarction incidence and
mortality.

\nMETHODS
Study population
The study population consisted of partici-
pants of the 1990 Nova Scotia Nutrition
Survey. A sample of 3,684 non-institution-
alized individuals between the ages of 
18-74 and stratified by age, sex, and coun-
ty were identified among registrants of the
Nova Scotia Medical Services Insurance.21
Among the 2,777 (75%) individuals who
were located, 2,198 (79%) individuals
agreed to participate and completed the
survey.21 Nine individuals were excluded
from the present study since they had a
myocardial infarction incident in the year
prior to the interview.
Dietary and risk factor assessment
The Nova Scotia Nutrition Survey was
conducted in 1990 and consisted of a face-
to-face interview, including a 24-hour
dietary recall questionnaire, a modified
food frequency questionnaire, and ques-
tions on demographics, socioeconomic sta-
tus, and other risk factors including smok-
ing and diabetes.21 Macro and micro-
nutrients in these individuals’ diets were
calculated using the Canadian Dietary
Information 
software 
program.21
Hemeiron was estimated as 40% of the
iron in meat, fish, and poultry.20,22-24 Body
Mass Index (BMI) was calculated by divid-
ing weight in kilograms by the square of
height in meters.
Health outcomes
All Nova Scotia administrative health
records from 1989 onwards are stored at
the Population Health Research Unit of
Dalhousie University.25 Incidence of non-
fatal and fatal acute myocardial infarction
(ICD-9 code 410) was obtained by linking
participants with these administrative data-
bases, including hospital discharge records,
physician visits, and vital statistics.
Information up to the end of the 1998 cal-
endar year was included in the analyses.
The linkage procedure also revealed out-
of-province migration of 206 participants,
and their information was included until
the date of migration.
Data analysis
We adjusted for the intake of iron and
hemeiron for the total energy intake
(iron/hemeiron intake per 1000 Kcal).26,27
This adjustment was suggested by Willet et
al. on the basis of a higher correlation
between subsequent nutrition surveys
when adjusted for caloric intake.28 We
divided study participants into tertiles
based on energy-adjusted intake of iron
and hemeiron. The lowest intake group
was used as the reference group. Age was
considered as a continuous covariate and
divided by 10 to quantify the impact of
10-year age increments. Similarly, energy
intake was considered as a continuous
covariate and the impact of 1000 Kcal
increments was examined. We applied
logistic regressions with myocardial infarc-
tion (nonfatal and fatal combined) as the
dependent variable. In initial analyses, we
adjusted for age and gender. In subsequent
analyses, we further adjusted for estab-
lished confounders including smoking,
BMI, diabetes, income, total fat, saturated
fat, and cholesterol. Sample weights are
generally applied in the analysis of surveys
with stratified sampling. For longitudinal
analysis of survey data with follow-up,
Korn and Graubard recommend adjusting
for the variables used in defining the sam-
ple weights (age, gender, and county) and
not incorporating sample weights.29 We
applied these recommendations in all
analyses. However, since county did not
substantially affect any of our estimates of
interest, we excluded this covariate from
our analyses.30
RESULTS
During the eight years following the sur-
vey, 94 (4.3%) individuals had an acute
myocardial infarction incident, of which
17 were fatal. Table I presents demograph-
ic and dietary characteristics of participants
with and without myocardial infarctions.
The study participants had a mean iron
intake of 6.95 mg per 1000 Kcal and a
mean hemeiron intake of 0.65 mg per
1000 Kcal (Table I). Adjusting for age and
gender differences, individuals in the high-
est iron intake tertile had 0.67 times the
risk of an acute myocardial infarction com-
pared to those in the lowest iron intake ter-
tile (95% CI of 0.40 to 1.15). Individuals

\nin the highest hemeiron intake tertile had
0.69 times the risk of an acute myocardial
infarction compared to those in the lowest
hemeiron intake tertile (95% CI of 0.41 to
1.17). In other words, the risk for myocar-
dial infarction is less among individuals
with high iron or high hemeiron intake,
although these differences are not statisti-
cally significant. Statistically significant dif-
ferences were obtained with respect to age
and gender: each 10-year increment in age
more than doubled the risk of myocardial
infarction, while females had 0.63 times
the risk of males. In addition, individuals
with diabetes and limited education had a
higher risk of myocardial infarction.
Smokers and individuals with low income
and high BMI also had a greater risk of
myocardial infarction, but the associations
were not statistically significant (Table I).
Table II presents the risk for myocardial
infarction associated with iron/hemeiron
intake when simultaneously adjusted for
the following confounders: age, gender,
smoking, BMI, diabetes, income, dietary
lipids, saturated fat, and cholesterol. The
risk of myocardial infarction for individu-
als in higher iron and hemeiron intake ter-
tiles was less than that of individuals in the
lowest intake tertiles, but these associations
were not statistically significant.
All the above results were almost identi-
cal when the analyses were further adjusted
for the length of follow-up as a means to
control for the 206 participants who
moved out of province (results not shown).
DISCUSSION
We found no increased risk for myocardial
infarction among individuals with high
iron or high hemeiron intake. Rather, indi-
viduals with higher iron and hemeiron
intake seemed to be at lower risk for
myocardial infarction, but these associa-
tions were not statistically significant.
Diet is cultural, and there are major dif-
ferences between countries and regions.
Therefore, it is important to investigate
dietary patterns and risks locally. Intake of
iron and hemeiron in the Nova Scotia
population appeared to be lower than in
the European study20 that reported an
increased risk of myocardial infarction
with increased hemeiron intake. The high-
er risk in the European study may be
attributable to high hemeiron intake and
high risk of nonfatal myocardial infarctions
in their highest tertile, since there were no
substantial risk differences between their
lowest and medium tertiles. With lower
hemeiron intake among the Nova Scotia
population, our study participants would
primarily fall in the lower and middle ter-
tiles of the European sample, with only
very few in their highest tertile. We specu-
late that this may be the reason that the
two studies have different results. With
respect to the risk associated with iron, our
results are consistent with those of a previ-
ous Canadian study among participants of
a nutrition survey conducted between
1970 and 1972,16 and with two other
North American studies among older pop-
ulations.8,9
The Nova Scotia Nutrition Survey was
conducted during spring and fall in order
to account for seasonal variations in diet.
The survey was also designed to obtain
representative samples from different age
groups, sex, and geographical regions of
the province.21 The study is further
strengthened by the high response rate and
the high follow-up rate that was estab-
lished through linkages with administrative
health information. In addition to demon-
strating the absence of a risk for myocar-
dial infarction associated with high dietary
iron and hemeiron intake, the study con-
firms the higher risk of myocardial infarc-
tion for those with diabetes, limited
income and education, smoking and high
BMI for this study population. A limita-
tion in this respect is our inability to adjust
for other risk factors including physical
activity, chronic diseases other than dia-
betes, family history of cardiovascular dis-
ease, and occurrence of a cardiovascular
disease incident prior to 1989.
Individuals with a high caloric intake are
more likely to have a larger amount of iron
and other nutrients in their diet.
According to Willett et al., individuals may
under- or overestimate their food con-
sumption, and thus, nutrient intakes may
be more appropriately estimated as a pro-
portion rather than an absolute amount.28
As pointed out by Hampl et al., consump-
tion of nutrients is partially dependent on
total energy intake, and the density of the
nutrient in the diet is more relevant than
the actual gross intake.26 An energy-adjusted
analysis may also be more appropriate in
terms of public health policy, as it is easier
for an individual to change food items
rather than to change their appetite.
Nevertheless, analyses of absolute iron or
hemeiron intake (not shown) revealed risk
estimates for myocardial infarction similar
to those presented here.
In Canada and most industrialized coun-
tries, cardiovascular disease is the leading
cause of death for both men and women.
In 1997, cardiovascular disease accounted
for 37% of all deaths, with 38% of the
deaths in women and 36% of the deaths in
men.31 In Canada in 1993, the direct costs
of CVD were estimated to be $7.27 billion
while the indirect costs were estimated at
$12.37 billion.32 In Nova Scotia in 1997,
1,589 individuals died from ischemic heart
disease, 806 of these from acute myocardial
infarction.31 The health of Nova Scotians is
among the poorest of all provinces and par-
allels poor lifestyle and socioeconomic fac-
tors.33-35 Clearly, the potential health and
monetary benefits associated with national
and provincial public health interventions
are tremendous.

\nThis study is the first study in Canada to
investigate the importance of both dietary
iron and hemeiron for the risk of myocar-
dial infarction. We found no increased risk
associated with dietary iron and hemeiron
intake, and thus there is no need for imme-
diate action towards changing the current
public health message promoting the con-
sumption of lean meat, which is rich in
iron and hemeiron. The current public
health message should be reconsidered if
the net benefits gained from reducing the
dietary iron and hemeiron intake outweigh
the risks associated with iron deficiency
and with greater intake of meat high in fat
and cholesterol. Since our findings are
based on the lifestyle and diet of Nova
Scotians, which is potentially different
from that of other provincial residents,
there is a need to repeat and confirm our
findings in other parts of the country.

DIETARY IRON AS A RISK FACTOR FOR MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION
RÉSUMÉ
Contexte : Des études épidémiologiques et expérimentales ont suggéré que de hauts niveaux de fer
diététique peuvent mener à un accident du myocarde. La viande maigre, une source importante de
fer diététique, est favorisée, grâce à un niveau de graisse et de cholestérol relativement bas. Cela
nous met-il en danger d’avoir un infarctus du myocarde et devrions-nous reconsidérer la promotion
de la viande maigre?
Méthode : Nous avons examiné la relation entre le fer diététique ou érythrocytaire et le risque d’un
infarctus aigu du myocarde parmi 2 198 participants d’une enquête alimentaire à la Nouvelle-
Écosse.
Résultats : Parmi ces individus, il y a eu 94 incidents d’infarctus aigus du myocarde pendant une
période de huit ans. Ayant ajusté pour les variables confondants, nous n’avons trouvé aucune
augmentation du risque d’un infarctus aigu associée avec une ration alimentaire élevée en fer
diététique et érythrocytaire.
Conclusions : Étant donné le style de vie et les habitudes alimentaires des Néo-Écossais, il n’y a pas
lieu de reconsidérer la promotion de la viande maigre.

Dietary Iron as a Risk Factor for
Myocardial Infarction
Public Health Considerations for Nova Scotia
Darshaka Malaviarachchi, MSc
Paul J. Veugelers, PhD
Alexandra M. Yip, MSc, OT(C)
David R. MacLean, MD
ABSTRACT
Background: Epidemiological and experimental studies have suggested that high levels of
dietary iron and hemeiron can lead to myocardial injury. Lean meat, a primary source of
iron and hemeiron, is promoted because it is lower in fat and cholesterol. Does lean meat
put us at risk for myocardial infarction, and should we reconsider its promotion?
Methods: We analyzed the importance of dietary iron and hemeiron as a risk for
myocardial infarction among 2,198 Nova Scotians who participated in a nutrition survey
and who were followed for eight years, using logistic regression.
Results: Acute myocardial infarction incidents occurred in 94 (4.3%) participants. We
found no increased risk for myocardial infarction associated with high intake of iron and
hemeiron.
Conclusions: Based on Nova Scotian data showing no increased risk for myocardial
infarction with high intake of iron and hemeiron, there is no need for immediate
reconsideration of promotion of lean meat.
A
large portion of the Western diet
consists of meat, and other parts of
the world are moving towards a
Western diet. Within the Western diet,
meat is the primary source of iron.
Recommendations for iron intake are 11 mg
for 14 to 18 year old males and 8 mg for
adult males.1 For females, recommenda-
tions are 15 mg for ages 14 to 18, 18 mg
for ages 19 to 50, and 8 mg for those over
50 years.1 These recommendations can
generally be met with a North American
diet.
Animal experiments have demonstrated
that high amounts of dietary iron can lead
to myocardial injury.2,3 In 1981, Sullivan
proposed that higher incidence of heart dis-
ease in men and postmenopausal women
was due to higher levels of stored iron.4 A
Finnish study in 1992 reinforced that
serum ferritin was associated with risk of
acute myocardial infarction.5 It has since
been shown that a high intake of iron and
cholesterol simultaneously could cause
more severe atherosclerotic lesions than
high intake of cholesterol alone.6 In addi-
tion, high iron levels may have a greater
impact on risk of myocardial infarction in
the presence of diabetes, hypertension, and
smoking.6 The various epidemiological
studies that evaluated serum iron levels and
dietary iron, however, have been inconsis-
tent with respect to the risk for myocardial
infarction.7-20 A recent European study sug-
gested that dietary hemeiron is associated
with increased incidence of myocardial
infarction.20 This finding may have impor-
tant public health implications because cur-
rent health promotion activities advocate
reducing the consumption of meat rich in
fat and cholesterol which implies the pro-
motion of lean meat. Lean meat has a high
iron content, of which approximately 40%
constitutes hemeiron. The promotion of
lean meat may have unforeseen negative
health consequences if hemeiron puts con-
sumers at risk for myocardial infarction.
Therefore, it is important to confirm the
findings of the European study, particularly
in settings that differ with respect to dietary
habits and lifestyle risk factors. In the pre-
sent study, we investigate dietary iron and
hemeiron in relation to the risk of myocar-
dial infarction in the province of Nova
Scotia, using the 1990 Nova Scotia
Nutrition Survey and eight years of follow-
up on myocardial infarction incidence and
mortality.

\nMETHODS
Study population
The study population consisted of partici-
pants of the 1990 Nova Scotia Nutrition
Survey. A sample of 3,684 non-institution-
alized individuals between the ages of 
18-74 and stratified by age, sex, and coun-
ty were identified among registrants of the
Nova Scotia Medical Services Insurance.21
Among the 2,777 (75%) individuals who
were located, 2,198 (79%) individuals
agreed to participate and completed the
survey.21 Nine individuals were excluded
from the present study since they had a
myocardial infarction incident in the year
prior to the interview.
Dietary and risk factor assessment
The Nova Scotia Nutrition Survey was
conducted in 1990 and consisted of a face-
to-face interview, including a 24-hour
dietary recall questionnaire, a modified
food frequency questionnaire, and ques-
tions on demographics, socioeconomic sta-
tus, and other risk factors including smok-
ing and diabetes.21 Macro and micro-
nutrients in these individuals’ diets were
calculated using the Canadian Dietary
Information 
software 
program.21
Hemeiron was estimated as 40% of the
iron in meat, fish, and poultry.20,22-24 Body
Mass Index (BMI) was calculated by divid-
ing weight in kilograms by the square of
height in meters.
Health outcomes
All Nova Scotia administrative health
records from 1989 onwards are stored at
the Population Health Research Unit of
Dalhousie University.25 Incidence of non-
fatal and fatal acute myocardial infarction
(ICD-9 code 410) was obtained by linking
participants with these administrative data-
bases, including hospital discharge records,
physician visits, and vital statistics.
Information up to the end of the 1998 cal-
endar year was included in the analyses.
The linkage procedure also revealed out-
of-province migration of 206 participants,
and their information was included until
the date of migration.
Data analysis
We adjusted for the intake of iron and
hemeiron for the total energy intake
(iron/hemeiron intake per 1000 Kcal).26,27
This adjustment was suggested by Willet et
al. on the basis of a higher correlation
between subsequent nutrition surveys
when adjusted for caloric intake.28 We
divided study participants into tertiles
based on energy-adjusted intake of iron
and hemeiron. The lowest intake group
was used as the reference group. Age was
considered as a continuous covariate and
divided by 10 to quantify the impact of
10-year age increments. Similarly, energy
intake was considered as a continuous
covariate and the impact of 1000 Kcal
increments was examined. We applied
logistic regressions with myocardial infarc-
tion (nonfatal and fatal combined) as the
dependent variable. In initial analyses, we
adjusted for age and gender. In subsequent
analyses, we further adjusted for estab-
lished confounders including smoking,
BMI, diabetes, income, total fat, saturated
fat, and cholesterol. Sample weights are
generally applied in the analysis of surveys
with stratified sampling. For longitudinal
analysis of survey data with follow-up,
Korn and Graubard recommend adjusting
for the variables used in defining the sam-
ple weights (age, gender, and county) and
not incorporating sample weights.29 We
applied these recommendations in all
analyses. However, since county did not
substantially affect any of our estimates of
interest, we excluded this covariate from
our analyses.30
RESULTS
During the eight years following the sur-
vey, 94 (4.3%) individuals had an acute
myocardial infarction incident, of which
17 were fatal. Table I presents demograph-
ic and dietary characteristics of participants
with and without myocardial infarctions.
The study participants had a mean iron
intake of 6.95 mg per 1000 Kcal and a
mean hemeiron intake of 0.65 mg per
1000 Kcal (Table I). Adjusting for age and
gender differences, individuals in the high-
est iron intake tertile had 0.67 times the
risk of an acute myocardial infarction com-
pared to those in the lowest iron intake ter-
tile (95% CI of 0.40 to 1.15). Individuals

\nin the highest hemeiron intake tertile had
0.69 times the risk of an acute myocardial
infarction compared to those in the lowest
hemeiron intake tertile (95% CI of 0.41 to
1.17). In other words, the risk for myocar-
dial infarction is less among individuals
with high iron or high hemeiron intake,
although these differences are not statisti-
cally significant. Statistically significant dif-
ferences were obtained with respect to age
and gender: each 10-year increment in age
more than doubled the risk of myocardial
infarction, while females had 0.63 times
the risk of males. In addition, individuals
with diabetes and limited education had a
higher risk of myocardial infarction.
Smokers and individuals with low income
and high BMI also had a greater risk of
myocardial infarction, but the associations
were not statistically significant (Table I).
Table II presents the risk for myocardial
infarction associated with iron/hemeiron
intake when simultaneously adjusted for
the following confounders: age, gender,
smoking, BMI, diabetes, income, dietary
lipids, saturated fat, and cholesterol. The
risk of myocardial infarction for individu-
als in higher iron and hemeiron intake ter-
tiles was less than that of individuals in the
lowest intake tertiles, but these associations
were not statistically significant.
All the above results were almost identi-
cal when the analyses were further adjusted
for the length of follow-up as a means to
control for the 206 participants who
moved out of province (results not shown).
DISCUSSION
We found no increased risk for myocardial
infarction among individuals with high
iron or high hemeiron intake. Rather, indi-
viduals with higher iron and hemeiron
intake seemed to be at lower risk for
myocardial infarction, but these associa-
tions were not statistically significant.
Diet is cultural, and there are major dif-
ferences between countries and regions.
Therefore, it is important to investigate
dietary patterns and risks locally. Intake of
iron and hemeiron in the Nova Scotia
population appeared to be lower than in
the European study20 that reported an
increased risk of myocardial infarction
with increased hemeiron intake. The high-
er risk in the European study may be
attributable to high hemeiron intake and
high risk of nonfatal myocardial infarctions
in their highest tertile, since there were no
substantial risk differences between their
lowest and medium tertiles. With lower
hemeiron intake among the Nova Scotia
population, our study participants would
primarily fall in the lower and middle ter-
tiles of the European sample, with only
very few in their highest tertile. We specu-
late that this may be the reason that the
two studies have different results. With
respect to the risk associated with iron, our
results are consistent with those of a previ-
ous Canadian study among participants of
a nutrition survey conducted between
1970 and 1972,16 and with two other
North American studies among older pop-
ulations.8,9
The Nova Scotia Nutrition Survey was
conducted during spring and fall in order
to account for seasonal variations in diet.
The survey was also designed to obtain
representative samples from different age
groups, sex, and geographical regions of
the province.21 The study is further
strengthened by the high response rate and
the high follow-up rate that was estab-
lished through linkages with administrative
health information. In addition to demon-
strating the absence of a risk for myocar-
dial infarction associated with high dietary
iron and hemeiron intake, the study con-
firms the higher risk of myocardial infarc-
tion for those with diabetes, limited
income and education, smoking and high
BMI for this study population. A limita-
tion in this respect is our inability to adjust
for other risk factors including physical
activity, chronic diseases other than dia-
betes, family history of cardiovascular dis-
ease, and occurrence of a cardiovascular
disease incident prior to 1989.
Individuals with a high caloric intake are
more likely to have a larger amount of iron
and other nutrients in their diet.
According to Willett et al., individuals may
under- or overestimate their food con-
sumption, and thus, nutrient intakes may
be more appropriately estimated as a pro-
portion rather than an absolute amount.28
As pointed out by Hampl et al., consump-
tion of nutrients is partially dependent on
total energy intake, and the density of the
nutrient in the diet is more relevant than
the actual gross intake.26 An energy-adjusted
analysis may also be more appropriate in
terms of public health policy, as it is easier
for an individual to change food items
rather than to change their appetite.
Nevertheless, analyses of absolute iron or
hemeiron intake (not shown) revealed risk
estimates for myocardial infarction similar
to those presented here.
In Canada and most industrialized coun-
tries, cardiovascular disease is the leading
cause of death for both men and women.
In 1997, cardiovascular disease accounted
for 37% of all deaths, with 38% of the
deaths in women and 36% of the deaths in
men.31 In Canada in 1993, the direct costs
of CVD were estimated to be $7.27 billion
while the indirect costs were estimated at
$12.37 billion.32 In Nova Scotia in 1997,
1,589 individuals died from ischemic heart
disease, 806 of these from acute myocardial
infarction.31 The health of Nova Scotians is
among the poorest of all provinces and par-
allels poor lifestyle and socioeconomic fac-
tors.33-35 Clearly, the potential health and
monetary benefits associated with national
and provincial public health interventions
are tremendous.

\nThis study is the first study in Canada to
investigate the importance of both dietary
iron and hemeiron for the risk of myocar-
dial infarction. We found no increased risk
associated with dietary iron and hemeiron
intake, and thus there is no need for imme-
diate action towards changing the current
public health message promoting the con-
sumption of lean meat, which is rich in
iron and hemeiron. The current public
health message should be reconsidered if
the net benefits gained from reducing the
dietary iron and hemeiron intake outweigh
the risks associated with iron deficiency
and with greater intake of meat high in fat
and cholesterol. Since our findings are
based on the lifestyle and diet of Nova
Scotians, which is potentially different
from that of other provincial residents,
there is a need to repeat and confirm our
findings in other parts of the country.

DIETARY IRON AS A RISK FACTOR FOR MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION
RÉSUMÉ
Contexte : Des études épidémiologiques et expérimentales ont suggéré que de hauts niveaux de fer
diététique peuvent mener à un accident du myocarde. La viande maigre, une source importante de
fer diététique, est favorisée, grâce à un niveau de graisse et de cholestérol relativement bas. Cela
nous met-il en danger d’avoir un infarctus du myocarde et devrions-nous reconsidérer la promotion
de la viande maigre?
Méthode : Nous avons examiné la relation entre le fer diététique ou érythrocytaire et le risque d’un
infarctus aigu du myocarde parmi 2 198 participants d’une enquête alimentaire à la Nouvelle-
Écosse.
Résultats : Parmi ces individus, il y a eu 94 incidents d’infarctus aigus du myocarde pendant une
période de huit ans. Ayant ajusté pour les variables confondants, nous n’avons trouvé aucune
augmentation du risque d’un infarctus aigu associée avec une ration alimentaire élevée en fer
diététique et érythrocytaire.
Conclusions : Étant donné le style de vie et les habitudes alimentaires des Néo-Écossais, il n’y a pas
lieu de reconsidérer la promotion de la viande maigre.

La séance a été ouverte par Mette Berger (MB- Lau-

Le patient brûlé présente un certain nombre de parti-

–
Perte de la barrière cutanée qui expose aux déper-
ditions thermiques, liquidiennes et accroît le risque
d’infections
–
Réanimation liquidienne précoce et abondante, ex-
posant parfois au risque d’apports excessifs qui peu-
vent entraîner des complications (« fluid creep »).
Par ailleurs l’œdème associé à la brûlure perturbe
l’évaluation correcte du poids du patient, expliquant
ainsi que ce n’est que vers le 15

e jour que le

–
Les besoins énergétiques et protéiques sont accrus
en raison de l’hypermétabolisme (catabolisme) ré-

brûlure.
–
Le tube digestif est agressé et pourtant il est im-
portant de le maintenir fonctionnel.
–
Il existe un déficit bien documenté en micronutri-
ments, avec notamment des travaux récents qui
concernent la vitamine D.
–
Les patients sont souvent en situation prolongée de
dépendance à la ventilation artificielle.
–
Les séjours pour brûlures sont volontiers de longue
durée (1 journée d’hospitalisation par % de brûlu-
re).
Le déficit nutritionnel peut s’avérer considérable. C’est

4 L’explication tient

Les formules fixes, type Curreri, sont à proscrire, car elles
n’adaptent pas les apports à la demande, variable comme

8 Pour les substrats, les recommandations sont les sui-

a retrouvé chez 80% des 37 enfants examinés une infil-

ces enfants étaient décédés d’infection).
9 Aucun parenchy-

les enfants de cette étude objectivent une vacuolisation
(macro ou microscopique) avec infiltrats associés. Le mé-
canisme en a été expliqué par une étude américaine (Fig.
2) qui met en évidence le rôle central des hormones de
« stress » qui provoquent une accélération de la produc-

tion de glucose pour répondre aux besoins de la cicatrisa-

10 Augmenter les apports glucidiques aboutit cepen-
dant à augmenter la production de triglycérides et d’acides
gras, stockés au niveau du foie. Cet effet délétère est ag-
gravé par toute atteinte hépatique septique. L’apport pro-
tidique s’inscrit dans une stratégie de limitation de l’éro-
sion de la masse maigre. Cette stratégie vise à promou-
voir l’anabolisme selon les bases suivantes : Moduler l’in-
flammation (SIRS), prévenir et traiter l’infection, éviter
l’acidose, complémenter en éléments trace, apporter des
hydrates de carbone et des protéines, maintenir la glycé-
mie entre 5 et 8 mmol/l par l’insuline, supplémenter en
acides aminés spécifiques, utiliser les hormones anaboli-
santes. La masse musculaire contribue à alimenter un pool
plasmatique d’acides aminés que la nutrition seule ne suf-
fit pas à enrichir (Fig. 3).
11 Ces acides aminés sont desti-
nés au fonctionnement hépatique mais aussi aux besoins
de la cicatrisation (brûlures + zones donneuses). Les be-
soins et le turn-over en acides aminés sont importants car,
non seulement tous les cycles métaboliques sont activés,
mais aussi il y a des pertes qu’il faut compenser. Ce turn-
over protéique est très important chez le brûlé, avec un
catabolisme (notamment de la masse musculaire) qui ex-
cède l’anabolisme pendant une très longue période. Les
flux d’acides aminés sont augmentés (arginine, ornithine,
leucine, proline, glutamine notamment), la conversion d’ar-
ginine en ornithine est augmentée, l’oxydation de l’argi-
nine et de l’ornithine est augmentée.
12 C’est ainsi qu’argi-
nine et glutamine deviennent des acides aminés essentiels
chez le brûlé (besoins en glutamine estimés à 0,3-0,5 g/kg)
alors qu’ils ne le sont pas chez le sujet sain. Pour l’ins-
tant seules les solutions contenant de la glutamine ont mon-
tré leur efficacité chez l’homme. Il est fondamental de mo-
nitorer la nutrition, notamment pour évaluer les besoins
caloriques, dont on sait qu’ils sont importants chez le brû-
lé, mais aussi variables au cours du séjour. En effet, le
seuil de dénutrition est différent chez le patient brûlé. Une
étude lithuanienne a montré que, sur 100 patients, ceux
dont les besoins nutritionnels étaient les plus importants
(>40 kCal/kg/J) présentaient la moitié des pneumopathies
et des infections.
13 Ce monitorage doit aussi impérative-
ment évaluer ce que le patient reçoit effectivement, c’est-
à-dire si l’apport calorique prévu a bien été délivré mais
aussi absorbé. Il est donc indispensable d’évaluer ce que
fait le patient de ce qu’on lui apporte. Les moyens à dé-
ployer pour manipuler la réponse métabolique sont le main-
tien d’une température ambiante à 28-30°c, l’excision-gref-
fe précoce, la prévention de l’infection et certains agents
pharmacologiques (β bloquants, insuline, oxandrolone, hor-
mone de croissance). Les β bloquants non sélectifs (type
propranolol) ont montré leur efficacité sur la réponse mé-
tabolique. Une étude américaine conduite par l’équipe de
Galveston, portant sur un collectif de 25 enfants brûlés sur
plus de 50% de la surface corporelle, a montré que, lorsque
le propranolol est prescrit durant 15 jours dans le but d’ob-
tenir une fréquence cardiaque 20% plus basse que dans le
groupe témoin, on observe que : la dépense énergétique
est significativement plus faible dans le groupe traité (cet-
te baisse persistant jusqu’à 2 ans après la brûlure ; le ca-
tabolisme est significativement réduit ( études isotopiques) ;
la sécrétion de catécholamines est abaissée, l’anabolisme
est augmenté, la prise de poids est augmentée (la masse
maigre augmente, la masse grasse augmente).
14 Les ana-
bolisants tels que l’oxandrolone (analogue non virilisant
de la testostérone) ont été évalués dans le cadre d’une étu-
de portant sur 150 enfants gravement brûlés (>30%SC).
15
Elle normalise quasiment la minéralisation osseuse et aug-
mente la masse maigre. Le contrôle glycémique a été éva-
lué car on sait que l’hyperglycémie obère la cicatrisation
des greffes.
16 Contrôler la glycémie en se fixant comme
cible 5-8 mmol/l (contrôle glycémique modéré) permet la
réduction significative des hypoglycémies (contrairement
à ce que l’on pouvait craindre) tout en évitant les hyper-
glycémies. Au total, les sociétés savantes recomman-
dent une nutrition entérale précoce adaptée aux besoins
(calorimétrie indirecte ou formule de Toronto) comprenant
un apport suffisant en éléments trace et agents antioxy-
dants, de moduler la réponse métabolique (bétabloquants
et oxandrolone), d’exciser et greffer précocement et d’éva-
luer la réponse au traitement nutritionnel.
Marie Reine Losser (MRL- Metz) a ensuite répondu
à la question : « comment évaluer les besoin calo-
riques ? ». La dénutrition et la surnutrition ayant un im-
pact majeur sur le devenir des patients brûlés, il est im-
portant de mesurer (plutôt qu’estimer) les besoins calo-
riques. C’est le rôle de la calorimétrie indirecte et donc
des calorimètres. La calorimétrie indirecte donne accès au
métabolisme de repos, qu’il est important de connaître car
Fig. 3 - Principes de la nutrition du brûlé, d’après 11.
